transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Markus (Helix CTO), Anita (Helix ML Infra), Tom (Helix Security), Jia (Helix Platform)

Summary:
Quick deep-dive on on-prem / air-gapped delivery: artifact delivery mechanics, offline licensing, GPU driver packaging, runtime knobs for latency vs throughput (KV cache, batching, quantization), and next steps to run a controlled pilot.

Topics:
- Artifact delivery and verification (tar bundles, checksums)
- Offline licensing and entitlement flow for air-gapped installs
- GPU driver packaging and offline vendor licensing (NVIDIA drivers)
- Runtime performance: KV cache sizing, batching policies, latency SLOs
- Quantization trade-offs and throughput gains
- VPC/on-prem integration considerations

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to do a focused deep dive on the air-gapped deployment for Helix. Carlos and Priya will walk through runtime and delivery.
[00:18] Markus: Yep, thanks Lena. We're real pressed for latency on inference, but also super tight on data residency and cannot allow any outbound calls, so the air-gapped option is the main path, wanted to confirm how offline licensing and drivers work.
[00:35] Carlos: Sure, so high level we'll provide an artifacts bundle that contains the runtime binaries, model artifacts, a small install shim, and checksums. For air-gapped installs we also provide an offline entitlement token which is a signed blob. The installer validates the signature locally.
[00:50] Anita: When you say signed blob, is there any PKI exchange required? We can't have any egress for key retrieval.
[00:58] Priya: Good question. The flow we use is pre-shared public certificate included in the bundle. The entitlement is signed by Redwood's private key. Installer has public key and verifies signature locally; no external key fetching. That’s the offline flow.
[01:14] Tom: How do you handle GPU drivers? Our security team requires vetted driver binaries, and in the past vendor licenses were a pain.
[01:22] Carlos: Right, GPU drivers are vendor-supplied; we don't relicense NVIDIA drivers. We package the recommended driver versions as a separate tarball and include SHA256 sums. Customer needs to accept NVIDIA EULA; we can provide the driver package as-is or guide you to provide your own vendor-provided RPMs/DEBs.
[01:36] Jia: Is there a signed checksum for the driver package as well? We want to verify integrity and tie back to the entitlement.
[01:42] Priya: Yep, every artifact (runtime, models, drivers) has checksums and we include a manifest file that's signed. Installer validates both the manifest and the artifact checksums.
[01:51] Markus: Ok that covers delivery. Now on runtime performance — our target P95 latency is 120ms on 8k context for our triage model, and we expect bursty traffic. How do KV cache and batching affect that?
[02:06] Carlos: Great constraints. Two levers: KV cache and batching. KV cache saves prefix keys on long-running sessions which massively reduces token compute when sessions are repeated, but it uses memory. If you keep kv cache in GPU memory you get lowest latency; if you spill to DRAM there's a hit.
[02:26] Carlos: In our on-prem runtime we allow configurable kv cache policies: in-GPU, host-ram with async prefetch, or disk-backed with eviction. For 120ms P95 at 8k, we'd recommend in-GPU kv for hot sessions and an LRU eviction tuned to session concurrency.
[02:42] Anita: What's the memory footprint per token? Rough numbers to guide GPU sizing.
[02:47] Carlos: Ballpark: kv entries scale with sequence length and model hidden size. For a 7B-ish model, expect ~2-3 bytes per token for compressed kv per head per layer after our quantized KV packing — hmm, that number can vary. I'd say plan for ~1.5-2 GB per 1k context in GPU for full kv in recent configs; we'll provide an exact calc for your model.
[03:09] Markus: That seems higher than our internal estimate, send us the calc sheet.
[03:12] Carlos: Will do. We'll run model-specific profiling.
[03:14] Priya: On batching: continuous batching improves throughput by aggregating tokens across requests; but it adds latency tail if you wait too long. We expose adaptive batching with max-latency and target-batch-size knobs. For bursty traffic we recommend small max-latency (e.g., 10ms) and opportunistic batching for background traffic.
[03:35] Tom: So for our P95 120ms target we should tune max-latency very low, maybe 5-8ms?
[03:40] Carlos: Exactly. Combine that with in-GPU kv to reduce compute per token; batching is primarily for throughput improvements on sustained load.
[03:48] Anita: What about quantization? We're curious how INT8/4-bit impacts latency and quality for our clinical triage prompts.
[03:56] Priya: Quantization reduces model memory and can boost throughput. Our runtime supports 8-bit and 4-bit paths. 8-bit often gives near-floating point (fp16) latency improvements with minimal quality regression. 4-bit has the biggest memory win and throughput, but there can be quality delta depending on the model and evaluation prompts. We'll recommend running a short eval suite on your clinical prompts.
[04:19] Markus: Can we run quantized variants and have automatic fallback to fp16 for flagged prompts?
[04:25] Carlos: Yes — we support per-route or per-prompt model variant routing. You can route sensitive or high-importance prompts to the fp16 variant and use quantized for less critical traffic.
[04:34] Jia: Any specifics about mixing kv cache with quantized runtime? Will the cache be compatible across variants?
[04:40] Priya: Good catch — kv cache encoding is tied to the model variant. Quantized variants produce KV encodings that are not always byte-compatible with fp16 variants. We offer a cache-compatibility mode where we store both keys or convert on the fly, but that costs memory/CPU. Usually we recommend keeping caches per-variant for simplicity.
[05:00] Tom: Security question: how is the offline entitlement enforced? Could someone copy the bundle and run unlimited?
[05:07] Carlos: The entitlement binds to a fingerprint — either a host machine ID, HSM-backed key, or a signed license file tied to a customer serial. Installer writes a local activation and enforces the license in runtime. For air-gapped installs we audit the activation; and we provide usage reporting file that can be exported for audits.
[05:24] Tom: Do you require any telemetry back? We can't have egress.
[05:27] Priya: No mandatory telemetry. We include local logs and an optional usage-blob that you can export to share with Redwood support. There is a telemetry opt-in if you enable it for managed support but for air-gapped customers it remains off by default.
[05:40] Markus: Ok, procedurally what's the pilot look like? We want to validate perf and integration within 2 weeks.
[05:47] Lena: Typical pilot is 2 weeks: week 1 install + smoke tests, week 2 run perf workloads. We'll provide a benchmark script and recommended test dataset. SE will lead install remotely with your platform team (offline share of artifacts).
[05:58] Anita: For the install runbook, do you automate kernel modules / driver installs or is it manual steps?
[06:03] Carlos: We provide both: a guided manual runbook and an optional installer script that applies drivers, runtime, and dependencies. For air-gapped we'll provide the script and all binaries; your infra team can review before executing.
[06:17] Jia: Are there special kernel versions required? We run a conservative kernel.
[06:20] Priya: We recommend kernels tested in our matrix; we'll include a compatibility table. If your kernel is older we can advise backports or using vendor driver packaging.
[06:30] Markus: Anything else on performance knobs — for tail latency do you offer pre-warm or pinned instances?
[06:35] Carlos: Yes — pre-warmed pinned worker pools are supported (pinning models to GPUs with reserved memory). That reduces cold-starts and keeps KV cached. For strict latency SLOs, pin a small pool for hot routes and use autoscaled pool for background.
[06:50] Tom: About fallback: if a GPU driver fails or a node goes down, what’s the graceful degradation?
[06:55] Priya: The runtime will redirect to a fallback model instance, either local host routes or a lower-sized model that can run on remaining GPUs. In air-gapped setups without external redundancy, we recommend multiple nodes and a canary/drain policy so you don't drop traffic.
[07:10] Lena: Great — I want to recap next steps and owners. Carlos will share the offline bundle and checksums, Priya will prep the benchmark scripts and compatibility table, Lena will share the licensing draft, Anita will provide perf test dataset. We'll aim for pilot start next week pending receipt of artifacts.
[07:30] Markus: Sounds good. Quick question — any blockers from Redwood re: NVIDIA licensing for distribution?
[07:36] Carlos: We cannot re-distribute vendor-licensed driver binaries under some agreements; in those cases we provide a stub and guide for you to download from the vendor and place into the bundle, or if permitted we'll include the driver tar with your signed acceptance. We'll make the approach explicit in the delivery notes.
[07:53] Anita: Please include explicit steps we can hand to security for review.
[07:57] Lena: Will do. Anything else?
[08:00] Jia: No, that's it from us. Thanks.
